newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE-Gulf coffers fill, economic reforms slow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Gulf coffers fill, economic reforms slow.

text.p: Oil prices are up and the coffers of the Gulf Arab states are filling with petrodollars.
Higher oil revenues -- estimated by economists and bankers at around $90 billion this year from $78 billion in 1995 -- are expected to help the six Gulf Arab states narrow their budget deficits.
But Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and United Arab Emirates, which sit on 45 percent of the world's oil reserves, cannot relax, economists, bankers and diplomats said.
They need to deliver on long-promised reform to a population growing by almost four percent a year if they want to attract private and foreign investment and compete in the global economy.

"The rise in oil revenue does not solve any of the fundamental challenges they face, be it cutting spending, creating first-class corporations, increasing private sector participation, reducing unemployment and downsizing the public sector," said Henry Azzam, chief economist at Saudi National Commercial Bank (NCB).

"It is hoped that the rise in oil prices would not lead to the reversal of the reform policies that were introduced in the past two years...If reforms are reversed or postponed, the region will lose the momentum for change that is already visible," he said.
Diplomats and economists in Kuwait were sceptical.
"Whenever oil prices rise, deficit pressure eases and enthusiasm to apply reform fades," said Kuwaiti economist Jassim al-Saadoun. Furthermore, "We start to increase spending."
"High oil prices have the effect of an aspirin on most Gulf states," said a diplomat. "They prefer it to surgery."
THE SLOW WHEELS OF REFORM
Oil will remain the Gulf Arabs' main source of income for many years.

"But governments now realise dependence on oil leaves them vulnerable," a Bahrain-based banker said. "They need to diversify and privatise...They need rules on greater financial transparency and to ease restriction on foreign cash to attract investments."

Most of the five-year development plans that take the Gulf states to the next century stress diversification from oil as a national goal. They talk of privatisation, employing more nationals, relying less on expatriates and less public spending.
But the process is proving slow.
"It does not mean they are not serious about the goals, but are being slow in taking them further," one diplomat said. "They need to send clear welcoming signals before private money comes."

Economists said Gulf countries had mixed feelings about a bigger private sector role, fearing social and political repercussions of the inevitably higher costs to consumers of privatised utilities, and concern over security.

They said the estimated $350 billion in Gulf money invested abroad underscored the predicament of Gulf states in pushing for a private sector role and attracting foreign investment to a region where most stock markets are illiquid, where financial disclosure is weak and foreign investment is restricted.
GROWTH FORECASTS GOOD

-- Saudi Arabia, the largest Gulf economy and the world's biggest oil producer and exporter, says reforms are beginning to bear fruit and it expects real gross domestic product growth of 6.2 percent this year compared with 4.2 percent in 1995.

Economists say it is probably using the extra oil revenue to build foreign reserves -- expected to grow to $11.8 billion in 1996 from $8.6 billion in 1995, pay debts to contractors and reduce the need for domestic debt to help finance its deficit.
It says it is reviewing its foreign capital law to introduce more incentives to lure foreign investors.
-- Oman, at the forefront of efforts to open Gulf economies, in November introduced amendments to its tax law, which had discriminated against companies with foreign shareholders.
The government's plan to the year 2000 forecasts annual nominal GDP growth of 4.6 percent. Nominal GDP grew 6.5 percent in 1995 and 3.4 percent in 1994.

-- The UAE, which plans to set up an official bourse in 1997, expects the economy to grow this year at around or slightly below 1995's real one percent. But economists warn that inflation, at around 12 percent, could negate any growth.

-- Qatar, also due to open a bourse in 1997, is banking on liquefied natural gas exports, due to start on December 24, as the engine of growth. The International Monetary Fund has forecast oil and gas exports would boost state income to $7 billion a year in 2000 from around $3 billion now.

-- Bahrain, the smallest Gulf economy, faces the huge task of tackling unemployment which is at the root of unrest. It predicts real economic growth this year of three percent and is optimistic the 1997-98 figure will be four percent.

-- Kuwait, whose economy was hit by Iraq's 1990 invasion, says firm oil prices helped it lift 1995 nominal GDP by 8.2 percent. Having recently paid off the last slice of a $5.5 billion loan, it can now face 1997 without the burden of foreign debt.
